title: Pillar 4: Metals, Reactivity Series & Redox Chemistry
subject: chem

questions.questionText: What is the oxidation state of sulfur in the sulfate ion ($SO_4^{2-}$)?

solution.formulaSetup: Sum of oxidation states in a polyatomic ion equals the ionic charge: $\text{OS}(S) + 4\text{OS}(O) = -2$.
steps: Oxygen normally has an oxidation state of $-2$.
Set up equation: $x + 4(-2) = -2$
Simplify: $x - 8 = -2$
Solve for $x$: $x = +6$.
solution.commonTrap: Equating the sum to 0 instead of $-2$ (which would give $+8$).

questions.questionText: Which metal in the reactivity series can be extracted from its oxide by reduction with carbon (coke)?

solution.formulaSetup: Carbon extraction boundary: Carbon can only reduce metals below it in the reactivity series ($K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al < [C] < Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu$).
steps: Metals above carbon ($K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al$) form very stable oxides and must be extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.
Iron ($Fe$) lies below carbon in the reactivity series.
In the blast furnace, iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon/carbon monoxide to molten iron: $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \to 2Fe + 3CO_2$.
solution.commonTrap: Choosing aluminium, which requires Hall-Héroult electrolysis because carbon cannot reduce $Al_2O_3$.

questions.questionText: What color change is observed when acidified potassium manganate(VII) ($KMnO_4$) acts as an oxidising agent?

solution.formulaSetup: Reduction half-equation: $MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \to Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$.
steps: Manganate(VII) ion ($MnO_4^-$) contains manganese in the $+7$ oxidation state, which is deep purple.
When it oxidises another substance, $MnO_4^-$ is reduced to manganese(II) ions ($Mn^{2+}$), which is virtually colourless in dilute solution.
Therefore, the observable color change is purple to colourless.
solution.commonTrap: Confusing $KMnO_4$ (purple to colourless) with potassium dichromate(VI) (orange to green).

questions.questionText: What is the primary reducing agent in the blast furnace that reduces iron(III) oxide to molten iron?

solution.formulaSetup: Blast furnace redox chemistry: $CO_2 + C \to 2CO$; $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \to 2Fe + 3CO_2$.
steps: Coke burns in hot air blast: $C + O_2 \to CO_2$.
Carbon dioxide reacts with more coke in an endothermic reaction to produce carbon monoxide: $CO_2 + C \to 2CO$.
Carbon monoxide is the principal gaseous reducing agent that reduces iron ores: $Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \to 2Fe + 3CO_2$.
solution.commonTrap: Selecting carbon (coke) as the main reducing agent throughout the furnace instead of carbon monoxide gas.

questions.questionText: Which of the following processes represents REDUCTION?

solution.formulaSetup: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons, Reduction Is Gain of electrons. Reduction involves decrease in oxidation state.
steps: In $Cl_2 + 2e^- \to 2Cl^-$, chlorine gains electrons and its oxidation state decreases from $0$ to $-1$. This is REDUCTION.
In all other options, electrons are lost (oxidation).
solution.commonTrap: Confusing loss and gain of electrons.

questions.questionText: What role does limestone ($CaCO_3$) play in the blast furnace during iron extraction?
options: It thermally decomposes to $CaO$, which removes acidic silica impurities ($SiO_2$) as molten slag ($CaSiO_3$)
It acts as a fuel to supply heat
It oxidises iron to prevent rust formation
It reduces carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide
questions.correctAnswer: It thermally decomposes to $CaO$, which removes acidic silica impurities ($SiO_2$) as molten slag ($CaSiO_3$)

solution.formulaSetup: Slag formation in blast furnace: $CaCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CaO + CO_2$; $CaO + SiO_2 \to CaSiO_3$.
steps: Limestone decomposes at high temperature: $CaCO_3 \to CaO + CO_2$.
Calcium oxide ($CaO$) is a basic oxide.
It reacts with acidic silicon dioxide ($SiO_2$, sand/silica impurities in haematite): $CaO + SiO_2 \to CaSiO_3$ (calcium silicate / slag).
Molten slag floats on top of molten iron and is tapped off separately.
solution.finalAnswer: It thermally decomposes to $CaO$, which removes acidic silica impurities ($SiO_2$) as molten slag ($CaSiO_3$)
solution.commonTrap: Claiming limestone directly reduces the iron ore.

questions.questionText: When iron nails are coated with zinc (galvanising), the iron is protected from rusting even if the zinc coating is scratched. Why?
options: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc oxidises preferentially, acting as a sacrificial anode
Zinc forms an impenetrable covalent polymer over iron
Zinc donates protons to iron to prevent oxidation
Zinc reacts with rust to convert it back to iron
questions.correctAnswer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc oxidises preferentially, acting as a sacrificial anode

solution.formulaSetup: Sacrificial protection mechanism: More reactive metal corrodes preferentially.
steps: Zinc is higher than iron in the reactivity series ($Zn > Fe$).
When the coating is scratched and exposed to water and oxygen, an electrochemical cell is formed.
Zinc loses electrons more readily than iron: $Zn \to Zn^{2+} + 2e^-$.
The electrons flow to the iron, preventing $Fe$ from losing electrons ($Fe \to Fe^{2+} + 2e^-$ is suppressed).
Thus, zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificed), protecting the iron underneath.
solution.finalAnswer: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so zinc oxidises preferentially, acting as a sacrificial anode
solution.commonTrap: Confusing galvanising with tin plating (tin is LESS reactive than iron, so if tin plating is scratched, iron rusts FASTER).

questions.questionText: In the reaction: $2FeCl_2 + Cl_2 \to 2FeCl_3$, which species is oxidised and which species acts as the oxidising agent?
options: $Fe^{2+}$ is oxidised; $Cl_2$ is the oxidising agent
$Cl_2$ is oxidised; $FeCl_2$ is the oxidising agent
$Cl^-$ is oxidised; $Fe^{3+}$ is the oxidising agent
$Fe^{3+}$ is reduced; $Cl_2$ is the reducing agent
questions.correctAnswer: $Fe^{2+}$ is oxidised; $Cl_2$ is the oxidising agent

solution.formulaSetup: Assign oxidation states: In $FeCl_2$, $Fe = +2, Cl = -1$. In $Cl_2$, $Cl = 0$. In $FeCl_3$, $Fe = +3, Cl = -1$.
steps: $Fe^{2+}$ increases its oxidation state from $+2$ to $+3$ (loss of electrons) $\implies Fe^{2+}$ is OXIDISED.
Chlorine gas ($Cl_2$) decreases its oxidation state from $0$ to $-1$ (gain of electrons) $\implies Cl_2$ is REDUCED.
The species that is reduced acts as the OXIDISING AGENT.
Therefore, $Fe^{2+}$ is oxidised, and $Cl_2$ is the oxidising agent.
solution.finalAnswer: $Fe^{2+}$ is oxidised; $Cl_2$ is the oxidising agent
solution.commonTrap: Confusing the species oxidised with the oxidising agent.

questions.questionText: Which of the following metal nitrates decomposes on heating to yield metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas ($NO_2$, brown fumes), and oxygen gas?

solution.formulaSetup: Thermal decomposition of nitrates: Group 1 ($Na, K$) $\to$ Nitrite + $O_2$; Moderately reactive ($Ca$ to $Cu$) $\to$ Oxide + $NO_2$ + $O_2$; Unreactive ($Ag, Au$) $\to$ Metal + $NO_2$ + $O_2$.
steps: $NaNO_3$ and $KNO_3$ decompose into nitrites: $2NaNO_3 \to 2NaNO_2 + O_2$ (no brown fumes).
$AgNO_3$ decomposes all the way to silver metal: $2AgNO_3 \to 2Ag + 2NO_2 + O_2$.
Copper(II) nitrate decomposes to metal oxide, brown $NO_2$, and $O_2$:
$2Cu(NO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2CuO + 4NO_2 + O_2$.
solution.commonTrap: Selecting sodium nitrate, which does not produce brown $NO_2$ fumes.

questions.questionText: What color change is observed when sulfur dioxide gas ($SO_2$, a reducing agent) is bubbled through acidified potassium dichromate(VI) ($K_2Cr_2O_7$)?

solution.formulaSetup: Dichromate reduction: $Cr_2O_7^{2-}(\text{orange}) + 14H^+ + 6e^- \to 2Cr^{3+}(\text{green}) + 7H_2O$.
steps: In $K_2Cr_2O_7$, chromium is in the $+6$ oxidation state, giving an intense orange colour.
Sulfur dioxide reduces chromium from $+6$ to $+3$ ($Cr^{3+}$ ions).
$Cr^{3+}$ ions in aqueous solution are green.
Therefore, the solution turns from orange to green.
solution.commonTrap: Stating purple to colourless (which is for potassium manganate(VII)).

questions.questionText: A strip of zinc is placed into an aqueous solution of lead(II) nitrate ($Pb(NO_3)_2$). What is observed, and what is the net ionic equation?
options: Grey crystals of lead deposit on the zinc strip; $Zn(s) + Pb^{2+}(aq) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + Pb(s)$
No reaction occurs because lead is more reactive than zinc
Effervescence of hydrogen gas; $Zn + 2H^+ \to Zn^{2+} + H_2$
questions.correctAnswer: Grey crystals of lead deposit on the zinc strip; $Zn(s) + Pb^{2+}(aq) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + Pb(s)$

solution.formulaSetup: Metal displacement reaction: More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its salt solution.
steps: In the reactivity series, zinc is higher than lead ($Zn > Pb$).
Zinc atoms lose electrons to become zinc ions: $Zn(s) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$.
Lead ions gain these electrons to become elemental lead: $Pb^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \to Pb(s)$ (grey crystalline solid).
Net ionic equation: $Zn(s) + Pb^{2+}(aq) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + Pb(s)$.
solution.finalAnswer: Grey crystals of lead deposit on the zinc strip; $Zn(s) + Pb^{2+}(aq) \to Zn^{2+}(aq) + Pb(s)$
solution.commonTrap: Thinking lead is more reactive than zinc.

questions.questionText: What color change is observed when aqueous potassium iodide ($KI$) is treated with an oxidising agent such as chlorine water or acidified hydrogen peroxide?
options: Colourless to reddish-brown (turns dark blue-black with starch)
questions.correctAnswer: Colourless to reddish-brown (turns dark blue-black with starch)

solution.formulaSetup: Oxidation of iodide: $2I^-(aq) \to I_2(aq) + 2e^-$.
steps: Iodide ions ($I^-$) in aqueous $KI$ are colourless.
When an oxidising agent is added, $I^-$ is oxidised to aqueous iodine ($I_2$).
Aqueous iodine produces a yellow-brown to reddish-brown solution.
Addition of starch solution confirms iodine by forming an intense dark blue-black complex.
solution.finalAnswer: Colourless to reddish-brown (turns dark blue-black with starch)
solution.commonTrap: Confusing iodide ($I^-$, colourless) with iodine ($I_2$, reddish-brown / purple vapor).

questions.questionText: Which of the following metals does NOT react with cold water or steam, but its oxide CAN be reduced by heating with hydrogen gas?

solution.formulaSetup: Reactivity with water vs hydrogen reduction: Metals below hydrogen ($Cu, Ag, Au$) cannot react with water or steam, and their oxides are readily reduced by $H_2$.
steps: Magnesium reacts slowly with cold water and vigorously with steam.
Zinc and iron react with steam when heated.
Copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series; it does NOT react with cold water or steam at all.
Copper(II) oxide can be reduced by hydrogen gas: $CuO + H_2 \to Cu + H_2O$ (black solid turns pink/brown).
solution.commonTrap: Selecting iron, which reacts with steam: $3Fe + 4H_2O \to Fe_3O_4 + 4H_2$.

questions.questionText: In an experiment, sulfur dioxide gas is bubbled into a solution of iron(III) chloride ($FeCl_3$). What is observed, and why?
options: The yellow-brown solution turns pale green because $Fe^{3+}$ is reduced to $Fe^{2+}$
The yellow-brown solution turns deep red because iron is oxidised to $Fe^{4+}$
A brown precipitate forms because iron is displaced
No change occurs because $SO_2$ is an oxidising agent
questions.correctAnswer: The yellow-brown solution turns pale green because $Fe^{3+}$ is reduced to $Fe^{2+}$

solution.formulaSetup: Redox reaction: $2Fe^{3+}(aq) + SO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l) \to 2Fe^{2+}(aq) + SO_4^{2-}(aq) + 4H^+(aq)$.
steps: Iron(III) ions ($Fe^{3+}$) are yellow-brown in aqueous solution.
Sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) is a strong reducing agent.
Sulfur dioxide reduces $Fe^{3+}$ to iron(II) ($Fe^{2+}$) while being oxidised to sulfate ($SO_4^{2-}$).
Iron(II) ions ($Fe^{2+}$) are pale green in aqueous solution.
Therefore, the solution colour changes from yellow-brown to pale green.
solution.finalAnswer: The yellow-brown solution turns pale green because $Fe^{3+}$ is reduced to $Fe^{2+}$
solution.commonTrap: Assuming $SO_2$ acts as an oxidising agent in this context.

questions.questionText: Balance the following redox equation in acidic solution: $\dots MnO_4^- + \dots Fe^{2+} + \dots H^+ \to \dots Mn^{2+} + \dots Fe^{3+} + \dots H_2O$. What is the stoichiometric ratio of $MnO_4^-$ to $Fe^{2+}$?

solution.formulaSetup: Combine half-equations by equalising electron transfer: Reduction: $MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \to Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$. Oxidation: $Fe^{2+} \to Fe^{3+} + e^-$.
steps: Reduction half-equation consumes 5 electrons: $MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \to Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$.
Oxidation half-equation releases 1 electron: $Fe^{2+} \to Fe^{3+} + e^-$.
Multiply oxidation half-equation by 5 to balance electrons: $5Fe^{2+} \to 5Fe^{3+} + 5e^-$.
Add equations: $MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \to Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$.
The ratio of $MnO_4^-$ to $Fe^{2+}$ is $1 : 5$.
solution.commonTrap: Equating mole ratios $1:1$ without balancing electrons transferred.

questions.questionText: A simple electrochemical cell consists of an iron electrode in iron(II) sulfate solution and a copper electrode in copper(II) sulfate solution connected by a wire and salt bridge. Which statement correctly describes the operation of this cell?
options: Electrons flow through the external wire from the iron electrode to the copper electrode; the iron electrode dissolves
Electrons flow from copper to iron; the copper electrode dissolves
Iron ions are reduced at the iron electrode; mass of iron increases
Sulfate ions flow through the wire from copper to iron
questions.correctAnswer: Electrons flow through the external wire from the iron electrode to the copper electrode; the iron electrode dissolves

solution.formulaSetup: Electrochemical cell: The more reactive metal is the negative electrode (anode) and undergoes oxidation.
steps: Iron is more reactive than copper ($Fe > Cu$), so iron has a greater tendency to lose electrons.
Anode (negative): $Fe(s) \to Fe^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$ (iron electrode loses mass / dissolves).
Electrons flow through the external circuit from the negative electrode ($Fe$) to the positive electrode ($Cu$).
Cathode (positive): $Cu^{2+}(aq) + 2e^- \to Cu(s)$ (copper electrode gains mass as copper deposits).
solution.finalAnswer: Electrons flow through the external wire from the iron electrode to the copper electrode; the iron electrode dissolves
solution.commonTrap: Claiming ions flow through the wire (ions only migrate through the electrolyte and salt bridge; only electrons flow through the wire).

questions.questionText: Disproportionation is a specific redox reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. Which of the following reactions is a disproportionation reaction?

solution.formulaSetup: Track oxidation states of the same element before and after the reaction.
steps: In reactants, chlorine in $Cl_2$ has an oxidation state of $0$.
In products:
In $NaCl$, chlorine has an oxidation state of $-1$ (reduced).
In $NaClO$, chlorine has an oxidation state of $+1$ (oxidised: $+1 + x - 2 = 0 \implies x = +1$).
Since chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, this is a disproportionation reaction.
solution.commonTrap: Confusing regular redox reactions (where two different elements undergo oxidation and reduction) with disproportionation.

questions.questionText: Three metals $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ were tested: (1) Heating oxide of $X$ produces metal $X$ and oxygen; (2) Metal $Y$ reacts with cold water; (3) Metal $Z$ reacts with steam but not cold water. Arrange $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ in order of DECREASING reactivity.

solution.formulaSetup: Deduce reactivity order from thermal stability of oxides and reaction with water.
steps: Metal $Y$ reacts with cold water $\implies Y$ is very reactive (e.g. $K, Na, Ca$).
Metal $Z$ reacts with steam but not cold water $\implies Z$ is moderately reactive (e.g. $Mg, Zn, Fe$).
Oxide of $X$ decomposes upon simple heating without any reducing agent $\implies X$ is very unreactive (e.g. $Ag, Au$, whose oxides decompose thermally: $2Ag_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} 4Ag + O_2$).
Decreasing order: $Y > Z > X$.
solution.commonTrap: Inverting the order to increasing reactivity instead of decreasing.

questions.questionText: Why can aluminium metal be used to manufacture window frames and aircraft bodies without corroding rapidly, despite being high up in the reactivity series?
options: Aluminium forms a tenacious, non-porous, impermeable oxide layer ($Al_2O_3$) on its surface that prevents further reaction with oxygen and water
Aluminium atoms form covalent bonds with atmospheric nitrogen
Aluminium is less reactive than hydrogen in real conditions
questions.correctAnswer: Aluminium forms a tenacious, non-porous, impermeable oxide layer ($Al_2O_3$) on its surface that prevents further reaction with oxygen and water

solution.formulaSetup: Apparent unreactivity of aluminium due to passivation.
steps: Aluminium is a very reactive metal ($Al > Zn > Fe$).
However, when exposed to air, aluminium rapidly reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough, non-porous, and firmly adherent protective oxide layer of $Al_2O_3$.
Unlike rust on iron (which is porous and flakes off), the $Al_2O_3$ layer is impermeable to water and oxygen, shielding the underlying metal from further corrosion.
solution.finalAnswer: Aluminium forms a tenacious, non-porous, impermeable oxide layer ($Al_2O_3$) on its surface that prevents further reaction with oxygen and water
solution.commonTrap: Claiming aluminium is inherently unreactive like copper or gold.

questions.questionText: In the Thermite reaction, aluminium powder reacts violently with iron(III) oxide: $2Al(s) + Fe_2O_3(s) \to Al_2O_3(s) + 2Fe(l)$. Explain this reaction in terms of oxidation state changes and energy considerations.
options: $Al$ is oxidised from $0$ to $+3$ and $Fe$ is reduced from $+3$ to $0$; the reaction is extremely exothermic, producing molten iron
$Fe$ is oxidised from $0$ to $+3$ and $Al$ is reduced from $+3$ to $0$; reaction is endothermic
Aluminium acts as an oxidising agent to burn iron
Iron displaces aluminium because iron has a higher melting point
questions.correctAnswer: $Al$ is oxidised from $0$ to $+3$ and $Fe$ is reduced from $+3$ to $0$; the reaction is extremely exothermic, producing molten iron

solution.formulaSetup: Redox analysis of Thermite welding process: $2Al + Fe_2O_3 \to Al_2O_3 + 2Fe$.
steps: Oxidation states: $Al(0) \to Al^{3+}$ in $Al_2O_3$ (oxidation state increases from $0$ to $+3$, oxidation).
$Fe^{3+}$ in $Fe_2O_3 \to Fe(0)$ (oxidation state decreases from $+3$ to $0$, reduction).
Because aluminium has a much higher affinity for oxygen than iron (higher lattice energy of $Al_2O_3$), the displacement reaction is violently exothermic.
The heat released is so immense ($>2500^\circ\text{C}$) that the iron produced is in the molten liquid state, used to weld railway tracks.
solution.finalAnswer: $Al$ is oxidised from $0$ to $+3$ and $Fe$ is reduced from $+3$ to $0$; the reaction is extremely exothermic, producing molten iron
solution.commonTrap: Stating that iron oxidises aluminium or that the reaction is endothermic.
